title: Clean code in Python
summary: Names, small functions, guard clauses, value objects and clear errors: refactor working code so others can read and change it.

lessons.title: Names that say what they mean
lessons.body:
# Names that say what they mean

Code is read far more often than it is written, and names carry most of its meaning. A good name says what a value is or what a function does, in the words of the problem, so the reader does not have to decode it.

```python
def calc(l, t):
    r = []
    for x in l:
        if x[1] >= t:
            r.append(x[0])
    return r

def passing_names(results, pass_mark):
    return [name for name, score in results
            if score >= pass_mark]

data = [("Ada", 81), ("Bo", 47)]
print(calc(data, 50))
print(passing_names(data, 50))
```

Both functions do the same thing. Only the second can be understood without running it.

- Functions do something, so name them after the action or the result: `send_invoice`, `total_price`.
- Booleans read as yes or no questions: `is_active`, `has_stock`.
- Collections are plural: `users`, `prices_by_item`.
- Avoid one-letter names and abbreviations only you know.
lessons.task: Rename `f` to `top_scorers(scores, count)` and give every local a real name: it returns the names of the `count` highest values in the dict `scores`, highest first, ties in alphabetical order. Rename `chk` to `is_passing(score, pass_mark=50)`, returning a bool.

checks.name: top_scorers keeps the behaviour
checks.code:
scores = {"cy": 90, "bo": 75, "ada": 90, "di": 60}
assert top_scorers(scores, 2) == ["ada", "cy"], top_scorers(scores, 2)
assert top_scorers(scores, 9) == ["ada", "cy", "bo", "di"], top_scorers(scores, 9)
assert top_scorers({}, 3) == [], top_scorers({}, 3)

checks.name: parameters say what they hold
checks.code:
import inspect
got = list(inspect.signature(top_scorers).parameters)
assert got == ["scores", "count"], got
got = list(inspect.signature(is_passing).parameters)
assert got == ["score", "pass_mark"], got

checks.name: no one-letter local names
checks.code:
local_names = top_scorers.__code__.co_varnames
short = [name for name in local_names if len(name) == 1 and name != "_"]
assert short == [], f"give these locals real names: {short}"

checks.name: is_passing returns a bool
checks.code:
assert is_passing(50) is True, is_passing(50)
assert is_passing(49) is False, is_passing(49)
assert is_passing(70, pass_mark=80) is False, is_passing(70, pass_mark=80)

hints: Work out what each name holds before renaming it: `d` is the scores, `n` is how many to return, and each `t` is one name and score pair.
`sorted` on a dict gives its keys, and the `key` function can look each score up: `-scores[name]` puts high scores first and `name` breaks ties.
`return sorted(scores, key=lambda name: (-scores[name], name))[:count]`, and `is_passing` is just `return score >= pass_mark`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter was correct, but every name had to be decoded from how it was used. `scores` and `count` tell a caller what to pass, and sorting the keys with a key function removes the index juggling of `x[1]` and `t[0]`.

`if condition: return True else: return False` says the condition twice. A comparison already is a bool, so return it, and let the name `is_passing` say what the bool means.

lessons.title: Small functions with one job
lessons.body:
# Small functions with one job

A long function usually does several jobs in a row: it parses input, checks it, computes something and formats the result. To change one job you have to read all of them, and you cannot test them apart.

Split it so that each function does one job and is named after it. The top function then reads as a summary of the steps.

```python
def parse_prices(text):
    parts = text.split(",")
    return [float(part) for part in parts]

def format_money(amount):
    return f"${amount:.2f}"

def receipt(text):
    total = sum(parse_prices(text))
    return format_money(total)

print(receipt("1.5, 2.25,3"))
```

## Signs a function wants splitting

- comments that announce sections, such as `# parse` or `# totals`
- blank lines between paragraphs of code
- a name with "and" in it, or no good name at all
- a loop that builds a value only the next block uses
lessons.task: Split `report(text)` into `parse_scores(text)`, returning `(name, score)` pairs with int scores and blank lines skipped, `average(scores)`, and `best_student(scores)`, returning the first pair with the highest score. `report` must call all three and return exactly the same text as before.

checks.name: report is unchanged
checks.code:
got = report("Ada,90
Bo, 70

Cy,85
")
assert got == "3 students, average 81.7, best Ada (90)", got
assert report("") == "no students", report("")

checks.name: parse_scores
checks.code:
got = parse_scores("Ada, 90

 Bo ,70
")
assert got == [("Ada", 90), ("Bo", 70)], got
assert parse_scores("") == [], parse_scores("")

checks.name: average and best_student
checks.code:
scores = [("Ada", 70), ("Bo", 90), ("Cy", 90)]
assert average(scores) == 250 / 3, average(scores)
assert best_student(scores) == ("Bo", 90), best_student(scores)

checks.name: report is built from the helpers
checks.code:
used = set(report.__code__.co_names)
missing = {"parse_scores", "average", "best_student"} - used
assert not missing, f"report should call {sorted(missing)}"

hints: Start with the comments in `report`: each one marks a job that can become a function.
Move the parsing loop into `parse_scores` and call it from `report`, then do the same for the average and the best row. Run the checks after each move.
`average` is `sum(score for _, score in scores) / len(scores)`, and `best_student` is `max(scores, key=lambda pair: pair[1])`, which keeps the first of equal scores.
lessons.explanation:
Each helper can now be tested and reused on its own, and `report` shows the whole plan in a few lines. The section comments disappeared because the function names say the same thing, and a name cannot drift out of date as quietly as a comment.

Move code in small steps and check after each one. A split that changes behaviour by accident, such as picking a different student on a tie, is much easier to spot one step at a time.

lessons.title: One level of abstraction
lessons.body:
# One level of abstraction

Inside a function, every line should sit at the same level of detail. A function that calls `charge(card)` and then slices a postcode by hand mixes the plan with its details, and the reader has to keep changing zoom.

Write the top function as the steps of the plan, each one a call to a well-named helper, and push the details down into those helpers. Read from the top, the file then goes from overview to detail.

```python
def make_slug(title):
    words = clean_words(title)
    return "-".join(words)

def clean_words(title):
    words = title.lower().split()
    return [word for word in words
            if word.isalnum()]

print(make_slug("Clean Code in Python"))
```

`make_slug` says what happens and `clean_words` says how. Python looks a helper up when the caller runs, so helpers can sit below the function that uses them.

If a step needs a comment to explain it, it is usually a helper waiting for a name.
lessons.task: Rewrite `signup(form)` as three calls: `clean_email(text)` (stripped, lower case, `ValueError` unless there is text on both sides of an `@`), `clean_name(text)` (capitalized words, `ValueError` if empty) and `greeting(name)`. `signup` itself must not call string methods, and it returns the same dict as before.

checks.name: signup returns the same record
bad input raises ValueError
the helpers
checks.code:
assert clean_email(" A@B.org ") == "a@b.org", clean_email(" A@B.org ")
assert clean_name("bo  DIDDLEY") == "Bo Diddley", clean_name("bo  DIDDLEY")
assert greeting("Bo") == "Welcome, Bo!", greeting("Bo")

checks.name: signup reads as the plan
checks.code:
used = set(signup.__code__.co_names)
missing = {"clean_email", "clean_name", "greeting"} - used
assert not missing, f"signup should call {sorted(missing)}"
string_methods = {"strip", "lower", "split", "join", "capitalize", "startswith", "endswith", "partition"}
leaked = sorted(used & string_methods)
assert not leaked, f"move {leaked} down into the helpers"

hints: Say the steps of `signup` in plain words: clean the email, clean the name, greet. Each step becomes a helper, and `signup` keeps only the calls.
Move the email lines into `clean_email(text)` and the name lines into `clean_name(text)`, each returning the cleaned value or raising `ValueError`.
`signup` becomes `email = clean_email(form["email"])`, `name = clean_name(form["name"])`, and a dict that uses `greeting(name)`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter worked, but to see what `signup` does you had to read string slicing and capitalization rules first. Now it is three lines that state the plan, and each rule lives in a function whose name says which rule it is. A change to email validation touches `clean_email` and nothing else.

The last check looks at the names `signup` uses: helper calls are what the top level should contain, and a string method there means a detail has leaked back up.

lessons.title: Guard clauses and early return
lessons.body:
# Guard clauses and early return

Nested `if` statements push the real work to the right, and an `else` can end up a screen away from its condition. Handle the special cases first, each with its own `return` or `raise`, and the main path runs unindented at the end.

```python
def shipping(order):
    if not order["items"]:
        return 0
    if order["country"] != "UK":
        return 20
    if order["total"] >= 50:
        return 0
    return 5

order = {"items": ["mug"],
         "country": "UK", "total": 30}
print(shipping(order))
```

Each guard answers one question and gets out of the way. By the last line, the reader knows every special case has been dealt with.

- Invalid input goes first, and raises.
- Then the cases with a fixed answer.
- Then the general rule.

Guards also make a new rule easy to add: it is one more guard, not another level of nesting.
lessons.task: Rewrite `ticket_price(age, day, member)` with guard clauses, keeping every price and error. Then add a new rule: children under 3 get in free (price 0).

checks.name: adult prices
seniors pay half
checks.code:
assert ticket_price(70, "sat", False) == 7.5, ticket_price(70, "sat", False)
assert ticket_price(65, "tue", True) == 4, ticket_price(65, "tue", True)
assert ticket_price(64, "tue", True) == 8, ticket_price(64, "tue", True)

checks.name: impossible ages raise ValueError
under 3 is free
checks.code:
assert ticket_price(0, "sat", False) == 0, ticket_price(0, "sat", False)
assert ticket_price(2, "mon", True) == 0, ticket_price(2, "mon", True)
assert ticket_price(3, "mon", False) == 10, ticket_price(3, "mon", False)

hints: Turn the two outer conditions around: `if age < 0: raise ...` and `if age >= 120: raise ...` go first, and the rest of the function loses two levels of indentation.
The free rule is one more guard, right after the errors: `if age < 3: return 0`.
After the guards, pick `price = 12 if member else 15` on weekends and `8 if member else 10` otherwise, then return `price / 2` for ages 65 and over.
lessons.explanation:
The nested version was correct, but each `else` sat far below its condition, and a new rule had no obvious home. With guards, each special case is handled and finished in two lines, so adding the free rule did not touch any other branch.

Order matters: errors first, so no price is ever computed for an impossible age, then the fixed answers, then the general rule.

lessons.title: Replacing flag arguments
lessons.body:
# Replacing flag arguments

What does `format_name("Ada", "Lovelace", True)` do? The caller cannot tell without opening the function. A boolean argument hides its meaning at the call site, and it often means the function does two different things.

There are two fixes.

- If the flag picks between two behaviours, write two functions whose names say which: `paid_orders(orders)` and `unpaid_orders(orders)`.
- If it is a genuine option, make it keyword-only by putting `*` before it. Callers then have to write its name.

```python
def format_name(first, last, *,
                last_first=False):
    if last_first:
        return f"{last}, {first}"
    return f"{first} {last}"

print(format_name("Ada", "Lovelace"))
print(format_name("Ada", "Lovelace",
                  last_first=True))
```

Now the call explains itself, and `format_name("Ada", "Lovelace", True)` raises `TypeError` instead of guessing.
lessons.task: Make `format_amount(amount, *, currency=False, estimate=False)` take both options by keyword only. Replace `order_ids(orders, flag)` with `paid_ids(orders)` and `unpaid_ids(orders)`.

checks.name: formats amounts
checks.code:
assert format_amount(1234.5) == "1,234.50", format_amount(1234.5)
assert format_amount(1234.5, currency=True) == "$1,234.50", format_amount(1234.5, currency=True)
assert format_amount(3, estimate=True) == "3.00 (estimate)", format_amount(3, estimate=True)
got = format_amount(3, currency=True, estimate=True)
assert got == "$3.00 (estimate)", got

checks.name: options are keyword-only
checks.code:
import inspect
params = inspect.signature(format_amount).parameters
for name in ("currency", "estimate"):
    assert name in params, f"format_amount needs a {name} parameter"
    assert params[name].kind is inspect.Parameter.KEYWORD_ONLY, f"{name} should come after *"
    assert params[name].default is False, f"{name} should default to False"
raised = False
try:
    format_amount(5, True)
except TypeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "format_amount(5, True) should raise TypeError"

checks.name: paid and unpaid ids
checks.code:
orders = [{"id": 1, "paid": True}, {"id": 2, "paid": False}, {"id": 3, "paid": True}]
assert paid_ids(orders) == [1, 3], paid_ids(orders)
assert unpaid_ids(orders) == [2], unpaid_ids(orders)
assert paid_ids([]) == [], paid_ids([])

checks.name: no flag left
checks.code:
import inspect
for func in (paid_ids, unpaid_ids):
    got = list(inspect.signature(func).parameters)
    assert got == ["orders"], f"{func.__name__} takes {got}, expected ['orders']"

hints: A bare `*` in a parameter list means that every parameter after it must be passed by name.
Rename the flags after what they switch on, `currency` and `estimate`, give them defaults of `False`, and put `*` before them. `order_ids` becomes two functions, one for each branch of its `if`.
`def format_amount(amount, *, currency=False, estimate=False):`, and `paid_ids` is `return [order["id"] for order in orders if order["paid"]]`.
lessons.explanation:
`format_amount(5, True, False)` worked, but nobody reading it knew what `True` switched on. Keyword-only options make the call say `currency=True`, and a third option added later cannot shift the meaning of calls that already exist.

`order_ids` with a flag was really two functions sharing a name. Two small functions, each named after what it returns, read better at the call site and need no `if` to work out what the caller meant.

lessons.title: Constants and enums
lessons.body:
# Constants and enums

A bare `50` or `"gold"` in the middle of a function is a magic value. The reader has to guess what it means, and changing it means finding every copy, including the one that is 50 for a different reason.

Give a number a name as a module-level constant, in capitals. For a fixed set of choices, use an `Enum`: a typo becomes an `AttributeError` instead of a silent mismatch, and editors can list the options.

```python
from enum import Enum

VAT_RATE = 0.2

class Tier(Enum):
    BASIC = "basic"
    GOLD = "gold"

def with_vat(net):
    return round(net * (1 + VAT_RATE), 2)

print(with_vat(10))
print(Tier("gold"), Tier.GOLD.value)
```

`Tier("gold")` turns stored text back into a member. Compare members with `is`, since each one exists exactly once.

Not every number is magic: `0`, `1` and `len(items) - 1` usually explain themselves.
lessons.task: Name the numbers `FREE_DELIVERY_FROM = 50`, `STANDARD_FEE = 4.99` and `SILVER_FEE = 2.5`, add an `Enum` called `Tier` with `BASIC`, `SILVER` and `GOLD` (values `"basic"`, `"silver"` and `"gold"`), and make `delivery_fee(total, tier)` take a `Tier` and use the constants.
lessons.solution:
from enum import Enum

FREE_DELIVERY_FROM = 50
STANDARD_FEE = 4.99
SILVER_FEE = 2.5


class Tier(Enum):
    BASIC = "basic"
    SILVER = "silver"
    GOLD = "gold"


def delivery_fee(total, tier):
    if tier is Tier.GOLD or total >= FREE_DELIVERY_FROM:
        return 0
    if tier is Tier.SILVER:
        return SILVER_FEE
    return STANDARD_FEE

checks.name: Tier is an enum
checks.code:
import enum
assert issubclass(Tier, enum.Enum), "Tier should subclass Enum"
got = [(member.name, member.value) for member in Tier]
assert got == [("BASIC", "basic"), ("SILVER", "silver"), ("GOLD", "gold")], got

checks.name: fees as before
checks.code:
cases = [(10, Tier.GOLD, 0), (60, Tier.BASIC, 0), (50, Tier.SILVER, 0), (10, Tier.SILVER, 2.5), (49.99, Tier.BASIC, 4.99)]
for total, tier, want in cases:
    got = delivery_fee(total, tier)
    assert got == want, f"delivery_fee({total}, {tier}) returned {got}, expected {want}"

checks.name: the constants
checks.code:
got = (FREE_DELIVERY_FROM, STANDARD_FEE, SILVER_FEE)
assert got == (50, 4.99, 2.5), got

checks.name: delivery_fee reads the constants
checks.code:
saved = FREE_DELIVERY_FROM, STANDARD_FEE, SILVER_FEE
FREE_DELIVERY_FROM, STANDARD_FEE, SILVER_FEE = 100, 7, 3
try:
    got = (delivery_fee(60, Tier.BASIC), delivery_fee(60, Tier.SILVER))
finally:
    FREE_DELIVERY_FROM, STANDARD_FEE, SILVER_FEE = saved
assert got == (7, 3), f"with the constants changed, delivery_fee returned {got}"

hints: Put the three constants at the top of the file, and write `class Tier(Enum):` with one line per member.
Inside `delivery_fee`, compare with `tier is Tier.GOLD` and use a constant's name wherever a number was.
`if tier is Tier.GOLD or total >= FREE_DELIVERY_FROM: return 0`, then `if tier is Tier.SILVER: return SILVER_FEE`, then `return STANDARD_FEE`.
lessons.explanation:
With names, the rule reads as a sentence: gold members and orders over the threshold pay nothing. When a fee changes there is one line to edit, and the last check proves that `delivery_fee` follows it.

The enum makes the set of tiers explicit. With strings, `"Gold"` or `"gld"` would quietly fall through to the standard fee; with `Tier`, a misspelt member fails the moment its line runs.

lessons.title: Comments versus clear code
lessons.body:
# Comments versus clear code

A comment that says what the code does is often a sign that the code could say it itself. Comments are never run or tested, so they drift: after a few edits, the comment says 30 days while the code says 45.

Before writing a comment that explains what, try:

- renaming a variable so the comment is not needed
- naming a condition, as in `is_adult = age >= 18`
- extracting a function named after the comment

Keep comments for what the code cannot say: why a choice was made, where a rule comes from, what a workaround works around. Docstrings tell callers what a function promises.

```python
ADULT_AGE = 18

def can_vote(person):
    """True for registered adults."""
    is_adult = person["age"] >= ADULT_AGE
    return is_adult and person["registered"]

ada = {"age": 36, "registered": True}
print(can_vote(ada))
```
lessons.task: Rename `process` to `amount_due(order)` with a one-line docstring, and turn its comments into code: extract `is_overdue(order)` and `with_late_fee(amount)`, and make `amount_due` call both.

checks.name: amount_due behaves like process
checks.code:
cases = [
    ({"amount": 40, "age_days": 31, "paid": False}, 42.0),
    ({"amount": 40, "age_days": 30, "paid": False}, 40),
    ({"amount": 40, "age_days": 90, "paid": True}, 40),
]
for order, want in cases:
    got = amount_due(order)
    assert got == want, f"amount_due({order}) returned {got}, expected {want}"

checks.name: is_overdue
checks.code:
assert is_overdue({"amount": 1, "age_days": 31, "paid": False}) is True, "31 days and unpaid is overdue"
assert is_overdue({"amount": 1, "age_days": 30, "paid": False}) is False, "30 days is not overdue yet"
assert is_overdue({"amount": 1, "age_days": 31, "paid": True}) is False, "a paid order is never overdue"

checks.name: with_late_fee
checks.code:
assert with_late_fee(40) == 42.0, with_late_fee(40)
assert with_late_fee(10.01) == 10.51, with_late_fee(10.01)

checks.name: amount_due uses the helpers
checks.code:
used = set(amount_due.__code__.co_names)
missing = {"is_overdue", "with_late_fee"} - used
assert not missing, f"amount_due should call {sorted(missing)}"

checks.name: amount_due has a docstring
checks.code:
doc = (amount_due.__doc__ or "").strip()
assert doc, "give amount_due a one-line docstring"

hints: Each comment names something: the first is a question about the order, the second a calculation. Those are the two helpers.
`is_overdue(order)` returns the condition from the `if`; `with_late_fee(amount)` returns the amount with 5% added, rounded to cents.
`amount_due` becomes `if is_overdue(order): return with_late_fee(order["amount"])` and `return order["amount"]`, under a docstring such as `"""Return what the customer owes today."""`.
lessons.explanation:
Every comment in the starter repeated the line below it. Now the names carry that meaning, and unlike comments they are tested: if `is_overdue` stops doing what its name says, a check fails.

The constants in the solution keep the 30 and the 5% in one place each. The one comment left explains where they come from, which is something the code cannot say.

lessons.title: Duplication and when to remove it
lessons.body:
# Duplication and when to remove it

When the same rule is copied into three functions, every fix has to be made three times, and one copy always gets missed. Write the rule once and pass in what varies.

```python
def labelled(items, label):
    names = ", ".join(sorted(items))
    return f"{label}: {names or 'none'}"

print(labelled({"tea", "jam"}, "Bought"))
print(labelled(set(), "Returned"))
```

Not all similar code is duplication, though. Two functions that look alike today but change for different reasons, say a tax rule and a shipping rule that both happen to multiply by 1.2, should stay apart. Merging them means that changing one breaks the other.

A useful habit is the rule of three: tolerate a second copy, and extract when the third arrives, because by then you can see which parts vary. Name the shared function after the rule it expresses, not after the code it happens to contain.
lessons.task: Extract `bulk_price(price, qty, min_qty, discount)`: `price` times `qty`, less the fraction `discount` when `qty` is at least `min_qty`, rounded to cents. Make `book_price`, `pen_price` and `paper_price` one-line calls to it, which also fixes the copy that forgot to round.

checks.name: same prices as before
checks.code:
assert book_price(12, 10) == 108, book_price(12, 10)
assert book_price(12, 9) == 108, book_price(12, 9)
assert pen_price(1.2, 19) == 22.8, pen_price(1.2, 19)
assert pen_price(1.2, 20) == 21.6, pen_price(1.2, 20)

checks.name: every price is rounded to cents
checks.code:
assert paper_price(0.33, 60) == 16.83, paper_price(0.33, 60)
assert paper_price(0.07, 3) == 0.21, paper_price(0.07, 3)

checks.name: the three call bulk_price
checks.code:
for func in (book_price, pen_price, paper_price):
    assert "bulk_price" in func.__code__.co_names, f"{func.__name__} should call bulk_price"

hints: Put the three functions side by side: only the minimum quantity and the discount differ, apart from one missing `round`.
Write `bulk_price` from one copy, replacing those two numbers with the parameters `min_qty` and `discount`, and keep the rounding.
`total = price * qty`, then `if qty >= min_qty: total *= 1 - discount`, then `return round(total, 2)`. `book_price` is `return bulk_price(price, qty, min_qty=10, discount=0.1)`.
lessons.explanation:
The bug in `paper_price` is the real cost of copies: rounding was there in two places and missing in the third. With one `bulk_price`, the rule exists once, and each product function only states its numbers.

These three merged well because they are one rule with different settings. If paper later got a completely different pricing scheme, it should stop calling `bulk_price` rather than add a flag to it.

lessons.title: From primitives to value objects
lessons.body:
# From primitives to value objects

Passing money around as a bare float, or as a tuple of amount and currency, spreads its rules everywhere: every caller must remember the unit, check the currency, and format it the same way. This habit has a name, primitive obsession.

A small frozen dataclass gives the idea a name and one home for its rules. It checks itself when created, so an invalid value never exists, and its behaviour lives in methods next to the data.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Money:
    cents: int
    currency: str

    def __add__(self, other):
        if other.currency != self.currency:
            message = "mixed currency"
            raise ValueError(message)
        total = self.cents + other.cents
        return Money(total, self.currency)

print(Money(150, "EUR") + Money(75, "EUR"))
```

Storing whole cents as an `int` avoids float rounding: `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`, but `10 + 20` is `30`. Two values with the same fields compare equal, which is exactly how a value should behave.
lessons.task: Replace the tuples with a frozen dataclass `Money(cents, currency)`. It raises `ValueError` unless the currency is three capital letters, `+` adds amounts of the same currency and raises `ValueError` for different ones, and `str()` gives text like `12.50 EUR`.

checks.name: Money is a frozen dataclass
checks.code:
import dataclasses
assert dataclasses.is_dataclass(Money), "use @dataclass(frozen=True)"
names = [field.name for field in dataclasses.fields(Money)]
assert names == ["cents", "currency"], names
money = Money(100, "EUR")
raised = False
try:
    money.cents = 5
except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "Money should be frozen"

checks.name: adds the same currency
checks.code:
got = Money(150, "EUR") + Money(75, "EUR")
assert got == Money(225, "EUR"), got

checks.name: refuses to mix currencies
checks the currency code
prints as an amount
checks.code:
assert str(Money(1250, "EUR")) == "12.50 EUR", str(Money(1250, "EUR"))
assert str(Money(5, "USD")) == "0.05 USD", str(Money(5, "USD"))

hints: Start from the example: `@dataclass(frozen=True)` with the fields `cents: int` and `currency: str`.
Checks on creation go in `__post_init__`, and `len(code) == 3 and code.isalpha() and code.isupper()` tests for three capital letters. `__str__` formats `self.cents / 100` with `:.2f`.
`__add__` raises `ValueError` when `other.currency != self.currency` and otherwise returns `Money(self.cents + other.cents, self.currency)`.
lessons.explanation:
The tuple version scattered its rules: `add_money` returned `None` on a mismatch, which callers could forget to check, and `show_money` printed `12.5 EUR`. Now `Money` refuses a bad currency when it is created and raises when currencies are mixed, so every `Money` in the program is a valid one.

Because it is frozen, a `Money` can be shared freely and used as a dict key: nobody can change the amount behind your back.

lessons.title: Prefer immutable values
lessons.body:
# Prefer immutable values

A function that changes the list or dict it was given surprises its caller, who may still be using it. Code that changes shared objects can only be understood by following it in time order.

Prefer to return new values:

- `sorted(items)` instead of `items.sort()`
- `{**prices, "tea": 3}` instead of `prices["tea"] = 3`
- tuples and frozensets for collections that should not change
- frozen dataclasses with `dataclasses.replace` for records

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    theme: str = "light"
    size: int = 14

base = Settings()
big = replace(base, size=18)
print(base)
print(big)
```

`replace` builds a copy with some fields changed. `base` is untouched, so anything holding it still sees what it saw before.

Changing an object your function created itself is fine. The rule is about values that other code can see.
lessons.task: Make `add_item(cart, name, qty=1)` return a new dict and `normalized(names)` return a new sorted list of stripped, lower-case names, both leaving their arguments untouched. Turn `Config` into a frozen dataclass with `host` and `port`, and add `with_port(port)` returning a changed copy.

checks.name: add_item returns a new cart
checks.code:
cart = {"tea": 1}
got = add_item(cart, "tea", 2)
assert got == {"tea": 3}, got
assert cart == {"tea": 1}, f"the original cart changed to {cart}"
assert add_item(cart, "jam") == {"tea": 1, "jam": 1}, add_item(cart, "jam")

checks.name: normalized leaves its input alone
checks.code:
names = ["  Bo", "al ", "Cy"]
got = normalized(names)
assert got == ["al", "bo", "cy"], got
assert names == ["  Bo", "al ", "Cy"], f"the input list changed to {names}"

checks.name: Config cannot be changed
checks.code:
config = Config("db", 5432)
assert (config.host, config.port) == ("db", 5432), (config.host, config.port)
raised = False
try:
    config.port = 1
except AttributeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "assigning to config.port should raise"
assert config.port == 5432, config.port

checks.name: with_port returns a copy
checks.code:
config = Config("db", 5432)
moved = config.with_port(6543)
assert (moved.host, moved.port) == ("db", 6543), (moved.host, moved.port)
assert config.port == 5432, f"the original port changed to {config.port}"
assert Config("db", 1) == Config("db", 1), "equal configs should compare equal"

hints: Build new values instead of changing the arguments: a dict display that starts with `**cart`, and `sorted` over a generator.
`{**cart, name: cart.get(name, 0) + qty}` copies the cart and sets one key, and `sorted(...)` always returns a new list.
Decorate `Config` with `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, declare `host: str` and `port: int`, and return `replace(self, port=port)` from `with_port`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter's `add_item` returned the very dict it received, so the caller's cart changed too, and `normalized` sorted before cleaning, which put `"  Bo"` first. Returning new values removes both surprises, and the caller decides whether to keep the old value.

A frozen `Config` can be passed to any function without wondering whether it comes back changed. `with_port` makes a change explicit and visible at the call site.

lessons.title: Pure functions, effects at the edges
lessons.body:
# Pure functions, effects at the edges

A pure function returns a result that depends only on its arguments, and changes nothing else: it does not print, write files, update globals or modify its inputs. Pure functions are easy to test, because a test is just a call and a comparison, and they are safe to reuse.

Programs still need effects. Keep them at the edges: a thin outer function reads the input, hands it to the pure core, and writes out the result.

```python
def count_words(lines):
    return sum(len(line.split())
               for line in lines)

def main(path):
    with open(path) as file:
        lines = file.read().splitlines()
    print(count_words(lines), "words")

with open("notes.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("one two\nthree\n")
main("notes.txt")
```

`count_words` can be tested with a list and no file at all, and `main` is so thin it hardly needs a test.
lessons.task: Write a pure `order_price(order)` and a pure `summarize(orders)` returning `(lines, total)`, with lines like `"order 1: 20"`. Make `print_summary(orders)` the only function that prints: each line, then `total: 25`. Use no globals and do not change the orders.
lessons.starter:
total = 0
log = []


def add_order(order):
    global total
    price = order["qty"] * order["unit_price"]
    if order.get("coupon") == "TENOFF":
        price = max(price - 10, 0)
    order["price"] = price
    total += price
    log.append(f"order {order['id']}: {price}")
    return price


def print_summary(orders):
    for order in orders:
        add_order(order)
    for line in log:
        print(line)
    print(f"total: {total}")

checks.name: order_price
checks.code:
assert order_price({"id": 1, "qty": 2, "unit_price": 10}) == 20, order_price({"id": 1, "qty": 2, "unit_price": 10})
assert order_price({"id": 2, "qty": 1, "unit_price": 15, "coupon": "TENOFF"}) == 5, order_price({"id": 2, "qty": 1, "unit_price": 15, "coupon": "TENOFF"})
assert order_price({"id": 3, "qty": 1, "unit_price": 4, "coupon": "TENOFF"}) == 0, order_price({"id": 3, "qty": 1, "unit_price": 4, "coupon": "TENOFF"})

checks.name: order_price changes and prints nothing
checks.code:
import contextlib, io
order = {"id": 1, "qty": 2, "unit_price": 10, "coupon": "TENOFF"}
before = dict(order)
out = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
    first = order_price(order)
    second = order_price(order)
assert order == before, f"the order changed to {order}"
assert first == second == 10, (first, second)
assert out.getvalue() == "", "order_price should not print"

checks.name: summarize
checks.code:
orders = [{"id": 1, "qty": 2, "unit_price": 10}, {"id": 2, "qty": 1, "unit_price": 15, "coupon": "TENOFF"}]
want = (["order 1: 20", "order 2: 5"], 25)
assert summarize(orders) == want, summarize(orders)
assert summarize(orders) == want, "a second call gave a different answer"
assert summarize([]) == ([], 0), summarize([])

checks.name: print_summary prints the same every time
checks.code:
import contextlib, io
orders = [{"id": 1, "qty": 2, "unit_price": 10}, {"id": 2, "qty": 1, "unit_price": 15, "coupon": "TENOFF"}]
for attempt in range(2):
    out = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
        print_summary(orders)
    got = out.getvalue()
    assert got == "order 1: 20\norder 2: 5\ntotal: 25\n", repr(got)

hints: Copy the price calculation from `add_order` into `order_price`, leaving out every line that stores or prints something.
`summarize` builds a fresh list and total on every call, as local variables, and returns them as a pair.
`print_summary` becomes `lines, total = summarize(orders)`, a loop that prints each line, and `print(f"total: {total}")`. Then delete the globals and `add_order`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter kept its running total in a global, so a second `print_summary` added to the first, and it wrote a `price` key into every order it was given. Those effects were mixed into the arithmetic, so nothing could be tested without them.

Now the arithmetic lives in two pure functions that a test can call any number of times, and the only effect, printing, sits in a three-line function at the edge.

lessons.title: Exceptions instead of error codes
lessons.body:
# Exceptions instead of error codes

Returning `-1`, `None` or `"error"` when something fails makes every caller check the result, and a forgotten check lets the failure flow on as if it were data: `-1` happily joins a sum.

Raise an exception instead. Callers that can handle the failure catch it, everyone else lets it propagate, and nobody can mistake it for a result.

```python
class OutOfStock(Exception):
    pass

def take(have, qty):
    if qty > have:
        message = f"want {qty}, have {have}"
        raise OutOfStock(message)
    return have - qty

try:
    take(2, 5)
except OutOfStock as error:
    print("cannot ship:", error)
```

Give a module its own exception classes when callers need to tell its failures apart, with one base class so that they can also catch them all at once. Put the details in the message, and in attributes when callers need the values.
lessons.task: Define `BankError(Exception)` with subclasses `InvalidAmount` and `InsufficientFunds`. `withdraw(balance, amount)` raises `InvalidAmount` for an amount of 0 or less and `InsufficientFunds` for an amount over the balance, instead of returning -1 and -2. `InsufficientFunds` keeps `balance` and `amount` as attributes.

checks.name: normal withdrawals
checks.code:
assert withdraw(10, 3) == 7, withdraw(10, 3)
assert withdraw(5, 5) == 0, withdraw(5, 5)

checks.name: bad amounts raise InvalidAmount
overdrafts raise InsufficientFunds
checks.code:
caught = None
try:
    withdraw(10, 15)
except InsufficientFunds as error:
    caught = error
assert caught is not None, "withdraw(10, 15) should raise InsufficientFunds"
assert (caught.balance, caught.amount) == (10, 15), (caught.balance, caught.amount)

checks.name: one base class for both

hints: Three small classes: `class BankError(Exception)` and two subclasses of it. A body of `pass` is enough for `InvalidAmount`.
Give `InsufficientFunds` an `__init__(self, balance, amount)` that calls `super().__init__(message)` and stores both values on `self`.
In `withdraw`, replace `return -1` with `raise InvalidAmount(...)` and `return -2` with `raise InsufficientFunds(balance, amount)`.
lessons.explanation:
With codes, `balance = withdraw(balance, 15)` quietly set the balance to `-2`. With exceptions, that line cannot complete: either a caller handles `InsufficientFunds`, with the numbers it needs on the error, or the program stops at the real problem.

The shared `BankError` base lets each caller choose its level: catch `InsufficientFunds` to offer a smaller amount, or `BankError` to report any banking failure.

lessons.title: One reason to change
lessons.body:
# One reason to change

A class or module should have one responsibility, which in practice means one reason to change. A report class that parses a file, applies business rules and formats text has to change whenever any of the three does, and testing its rules means building a file first.

```python
class Invoice:
    def __init__(self, lines):
        self.lines = lines

    def total(self):
        total = 0
        for qty, price in self.lines:
            total += qty * price
        return total

def render(invoice):
    return f"Total: {invoice.total():.2f}"

print(render(Invoice([(2, 1.5), (1, 4.0)])))
```

`Invoice` knows the rules and `render` knows the layout. A new layout leaves `Invoice` alone.

## Refactoring in small steps

Pin the current behaviour with tests, move one piece out, run the tests, and repeat. Every step leaves working code, so you can stop at any point.
lessons.task: Split `SalesReport` into `parse_sales(csv_text)` returning `(region, amount)` pairs, a class `SalesTotals(rows)` whose `by_region()` returns a dict of sums, and `render_totals(totals)` producing the old text. `sales_report(csv_text)` connects them and returns what `SalesReport(csv_text).text()` did.

checks.name: parse_sales
checks.code:
text = "region,amount
north,10
south,2.5
north,1
"
got = parse_sales(text)
assert got == [("north", 10.0), ("south", 2.5), ("north", 1.0)], got
assert parse_sales("region,amount
") == [], parse_sales("region,amount
")

checks.name: SalesTotals sums by region
checks.code:
totals = SalesTotals([("n", 1.0), ("s", 2.0), ("n", 3.0)])
assert totals.by_region() == {"n": 4.0, "s": 2.0}, totals.by_region()
assert SalesTotals([]).by_region() == {}, SalesTotals([]).by_region()

checks.name: render_totals
checks.code:
got = render_totals({"south": 2.5, "north": 11.0})
assert got == "north: 11.00\nsouth: 2.50", repr(got)

checks.name: sales_report gives the old text
checks.code:
got = sales_report("region,amount
north,10
south,2.5
north,1
")
assert got == "north: 11.00
south: 2.50", repr(got)
used = set(sales_report.__code__.co_names)
missing = {"parse_sales", "SalesTotals", "render_totals"} - used
assert not missing, f"sales_report should use {sorted(missing)}"

hints: Look for what could change independently: the input format, the summing rule and the output layout. Each gets its own home.
Move the parsing loop from `__init__` into `parse_sales`, the summing loop into `SalesTotals.by_region`, and the formatting loop into `render_totals`.
`sales_report` is `render_totals(SalesTotals(parse_sales(csv_text)).by_region())`, split over two lines if you like.
lessons.explanation:
In the starter, testing the sums meant writing CSV text, and switching the input to JSON would have meant editing the class that also formats the output. After the split, each piece has one reason to change and can be tested with plain Python values.

`SalesTotals` is a class because it is the part most likely to grow: averages, the best region, filters. Parsing and rendering are single functions, and that is fine: a responsibility does not need a class.

lessons.title: Open for extension
lessons.task: Replace the chain with a registry: a dict `DISCOUNTS`, a decorator `discount_rule(name)` that stores a function in it and returns the function unchanged, one function per kind, and `apply_discount(kind, total)` that looks the rule up, raising `ValueError` for an unknown kind. Then add `"fifth_off"`, which takes 20% off.

checks.name: existing discounts
checks.code:
cases = [("none", 40, 40), ("half", 40, 20), ("ten_off", 40, 30), ("ten_off", 5, 0)]
for kind, total, want in cases:
    got = apply_discount(kind, total)
    assert got == want, f"apply_discount({kind!r}, {total}) returned {got}, expected {want}"

checks.name: the new fifth_off rule
checks.code: assert apply_discount("fifth_off", 50) == 40, apply_discount("fifth_off", 50)

checks.name: unknown kinds raise ValueError
rules live in DISCOUNTS
a new rule needs no edits

hints: Copy the registry from the example and rename it: `DISCOUNTS = {}` and a `discount_rule(name)` decorator whose inner function stores the rule and returns it.
Give each branch of the chain its own decorated function taking `total`. `apply_discount` then only looks up `DISCOUNTS[kind]` and calls it.
Turn the `KeyError` from a missing kind into `raise ValueError(...) from None`, and add `@discount_rule("fifth_off")` above a function that returns `total * 0.8`.
lessons.explanation:
In the chain, every new discount meant editing `apply_discount` and risking the branches next to it. With the registry, `apply_discount` is finished: the last check registered a `free` rule from outside your code, and it worked without changing anything.

The decorator must return the function, or the decorated name becomes `None`. Classes give the same shape: each kind is a class with an `apply` method, and the caller calls `rule.apply(total)` without asking which kind it has.

lessons.title: Type hints as documentation
lessons.body:
# Type hints as documentation

A signature is the first thing a reader sees. `def find(users, key)` leaves every question open. With hints, the signature answers them: what to pass, what comes back, and whether it can be missing.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class User:
    email: str
    name: str

def find_user(users: list[User],
              email: str) -> User | None:
    for user in users:
        if user.email == email:
            return user
    return None

ada = User("ada@x.org", "Ada")
print(find_user([ada], "ada@x.org"))
```

`-> User | None` warns every caller to handle the missing case, and a type checker flags one that does not.

Hints are not checked when the code runs, but unlike comments they are read by editors and checkers, so a stale hint gets noticed. Make them precise: `dict[int, list[str]]` says far more than `dict`. And let them steer the design: returning an empty list instead of `None` removes the `| None`, and every check that came with it.
lessons.task: Move the comments into the signatures: `tags_for(tags_by_user: dict[int, list[str]], user_id: int) -> list[str]`, returning an empty list for an unknown user, and `most_tagged(tags_by_user: dict[int, list[str]]) -> int | None`.

checks.name: tags_for has exact hints
checks.code:
import typing
hints = typing.get_type_hints(tags_for)
want = {"tags_by_user": dict[int, list[str]], "user_id": int, "return": list[str]}
assert hints == want, hints

checks.name: tags_for always returns a list
checks.code:
index = {1: ["admin", "beta"], 2: []}
assert tags_for(index, 1) == ["admin", "beta"], tags_for(index, 1)
assert tags_for(index, 2) == [], tags_for(index, 2)
assert tags_for(index, 3) == [], tags_for(index, 3)

checks.name: most_tagged has exact hints
checks.code:
import typing
hints = typing.get_type_hints(most_tagged)
want = {"tags_by_user": dict[int, list[str]], "return": int | None}
assert hints == want, hints

checks.name: most_tagged behaviour
checks.code:
assert most_tagged({1: ["a"], 2: ["a", "b"]}) == 2, most_tagged({1: ["a"], 2: ["a", "b"]})
assert most_tagged({5: ["a"], 7: ["b"]}) == 5, most_tagged({5: ["a"], 7: ["b"]})
assert most_tagged({}) is None, most_tagged({})

hints: Turn each comment into a hint: a dict from `int` to a list of strings is written `dict[int, list[str]]`.
Rename `db` and `uid` to `tags_by_user` and `user_id` as you go. The names and the hints together replace the comments.
`tags_for` returns `tags_by_user.get(user_id, [])`, so its return hint is plain `list[str]`; `most_tagged` keeps its `None` case and returns `int | None`.
lessons.explanation:
The comments said what the hints now say, but nothing read them. An editor shows the hints whenever you call `tags_for`, and a checker warns if someone passes a user name instead of an id.

Changing the unknown-user result from `None` to `[]` let the hint say `list[str]`, so callers can loop over the result directly. `most_tagged` has no sensible answer for an empty dict, so its `int | None` is honest, and the hint makes every caller deal with it.
